title: Ventricular Pulsed Field Ablation: State-of-the-art Review of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence.
summary: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a paradigm shift in the field of cardiac electrophysiology. The well-demonstrated success with atrial PFA is generating enthusiasm for ventricular applications of PFA, for which the clinical experience is still in its infancy, however. This study is a systematic review and critical appraisal of the published preclinical and clinical evidence on ventricular PFA, involving a total of 111 primary articles (55 preclinical and 56 clinical). An increasing number of PFA platforms and catheters are being used in the ventricle in clinical practice. This appraisal evaluates the impact of ablation parameters in association with lesion depth and volume, and synthesises the available studies of safety and efficacy outcomes for ablation of ventricular tachycardia and premature ventricular complexes with PFA, as reported in case reports and case series from around the world. The cumulative published evidence amounts to a total of 434 patients ablated with PFA for ventricular arrhythmias, with generally favourable acute and long-term results, while the understanding of safety constraints continues to be explored.

title: Association of Mean Left Atrial Pressure With Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation: Subanalysis of the Shinshu Catheter Ablation (Shinshu-AB) Registry.
summary:
BACKGROUND: The association of invasively measured mean left atrial pressure (LAP) during catheter ablation (CA) for atrial fibrillation (AF) with clinical characteristics and outcomes remains unclear.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We analyzed the data of 480 patients from the Shinshu Catheter Ablation Registry who underwent CA for AF (median age, 69 years; 146 women [30.4%]; 207 patients [43.1%] with persistent AF). Patients were categorized by mean LAP as normal (<12 mmHg; n=318 [66.3%]), mildly elevated (12 to <15 mmHg; n=78 [16.3%]), or elevated (≥15 mmHg; n=84 [17.5%]). Study endpoints were early AF recurrence within the 8-week blanking period, late AF recurrence, and composite adverse clinical events (heart failure hospitalization, symptomatic stroke, or all-cause death) during the 1-year follow-up after CA. Patients in the higher LAP groups had a higher prevalence of obesity and persistent AF, and a larger left atrial volume index. Early AF recurrence differed significantly across the LAP groups and was highest in the elevated LAP group (log-rank P=0.017). After multivariable adjustment, early AF recurrence risk increased across the LAP groups (hazard ratio per-category increase, 1.41; 95% confidence interval, 1.04-1.90; P for trend=0.028). In contrast, late AF recurrence and composite adverse clinical events did not differ significantly across the LAP groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Mean LAP during CA for AF was associated with AF-related clinical characteristics and early AF recurrence.

title: Leadless Pacemaker Implantation in Fabry Disease With Permanent Atrial Fibrillation and Bradycardia: Diagnostic and Implantation Guidance by Preprocedural Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
summary: In advanced Fabry cardiomyopathy, preprocedural cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may reveal a lower septal region spared from otherwise extensive septal late gadolinium enhancement. This information, combined with pre-fixation electrical mapping, may help identify an optimal site for leadless pacemaker implantation and minimize repeated fixation attempts.

title: [German Society of Cardiology position paper-how to treat patients with electrical storm: executive summary].
summary: Electrical storm (ES), defined as at least three sustained episodes of ventricular arrhythmia within 24 h, is a life-threatening state of electrical and frequently hemodynamic instability associated with a high risk of mortality. Recurrent ventricular arrhythmias indicate prognostically relevant disease progression even before overt ES develops. Accordingly, ES often represents the culmination of a continuum of increasing electrical instability that should ideally be prevented or interrupted at an early stage. Characterization of the underlying arrhythmogenic substrate, arrhythmogenic triggers, and the arrhythmia itself, together with assessment of the overall hemodynamic status, forms the basis for risk stratification, diagnostic evaluation, and targeted treatment of ES. For the first time, the German Cardiac Society (DGK) position paper integrates these three dimensions-substrate, trigger, and arrhythmia (STA)-into the STA triad. Most episodes of ES occur in patients with structural heart disease, particularly ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy with advanced heart failure; primary electrical or inherited arrhythmia syndromes are less common. The NHII-MED (neuroendocrine dysfunction, heart failure/hemodynamics, ischemia/coronary pathology, inflammation/infection, medication/metabolic factors, electrolyte imbalances, drugs/alcohol) framework was introduced to facilitate systematic trigger identification and management. Core components of specialized acute treatment include correction of reversible causes, device management including implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) reprogramming, antiarrhythmic drug therapy, sedation, catheter ablation, autonomic modulation, optimization of treatment for the underlying cardiac disease, and, when required, mechanical circulatory support. The overarching therapeutic objective is to prevent further ventricular arrhythmias and repetitive ICD therapies. This executive summary of the DGK position paper addresses the associated clinical challenges and contemporary management options.

title: Bridging of Finger-Prick Volumetric Absorptive Microsampling and Conventional Venous Sampling with Clinical Specimens for Direct Oral Anticoagulants Analysis by LC-MS/MS.
summary:
OBJECTIVES: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the first-line therapy for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Exposure-response analysis has shown correlations between drug concentrations and clinical outcomes, making therapeutic drug monitoring a valuable tool. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) enables sensitive and accurate quantification for clinical analysis. Volumetric absorptive microsampling (VAMS) is a minimally invasive technique for collecting dried blood specimens. However, the translation from conventional venous blood sampling to VAMS and the conversion between plasma and whole-blood concentrations remain unclear.

METHODS: We developed an LC-MS/MS method for quantifying four DOACs-dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban, and edoxaban-in VAMS samples and applied it to paired clinical specimens to compare venous and finger-prick blood and establish conversion factors.

RESULTS: Validation results support accuracy and precision of VAMS analysis by LC-MS/MS. Comparative analysis demonstrated no significant differences in concentrations between finger-prick and venous blood for dabigatran, apixaban, and rivaroxaban. Using paired clinical samples, conversion factors were derived via weighted Deming regression: 1.88, 1.57, 1.64, and 1.08 for dabigatran (n = 30), rivaroxaban (n = 33), apixaban (n = 35), and edoxaban (n = 36), respectively. The hematocrit effect was statistically significant for dabigatran. Bland-Altman analysis showed that more than 80% of samples fell within ±20% of the mean between estimated and measured plasma concentrations.

CONCLUSION: These findings support the potential clinical utility of VAMS with LC-MS/MS as an accurate and convenient tool for DOAC monitoring, facilitating future implementation of precision medicine in anticoagulation management to minimize bleeding and stroke events.

title: Association between nursing assessment indicators and adverse outcomes in hospitalized patients with atrial fibrillation: A retrospective observational study.
summary: This retrospective observational study examines the association between routinely collected admission nursing assessment indicators and in-hospital adverse outcomes among hospitalized patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). A total of 312 hospitalized patients with AF admitted to a tertiary teaching hospital between January 2021 and December 2024 were included. The Morse Fall Scale, Barthel Index, Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 (NRS-2002), and Braden Scale were assessed within 24 hours of admission. Clinical characteristics, vital signs, and laboratory data were extracted from electronic medical records. The composite adverse outcome comprised in-hospital death, unplanned intensive care unit admission, worsening heart failure requiring treatment escalation, major bleeding requiring medical intervention, or thromboembolic events. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to examine associations with the composite outcome. Among 312 patients, 68 (21.8%) experienced at least one adverse outcome. In the adjusted analysis, a higher Morse Fall Scale score was associated with higher odds of adverse outcomes (OR 1.031, 95% CI 1.012-1.051; P = .002), whereas a higher Barthel Index score was associated with lower odds (OR 0.978, 95% CI 0.961-0.995; P = .012). A higher NRS-2002 score was associated with higher odds (OR 1.376, 95% CI 1.083-1.748; P = .009), and a higher serum albumin level was associated with lower odds (OR 0.953, 95% CI 0.920-0.988; P = .010). AF type and Braden Scale score were not independently associated with the composite outcome after adjustment. Admission nursing assessments of fall risk, functional status, and nutritional risk, together with serum albumin, were independently associated with in-hospital adverse outcomes. These results support their use as complementary markers of vulnerability and for closer clinical surveillance, but they do not establish causality or justify changing guideline-directed AF treatment. Prospective multicenter studies are required before these measures can be incorporated into validated clinical decision tools.

title: Persistent atrial fibrillation in older adults: Comparison of seven models and development of a gradient boosting machine classifier in a single-center observational study.
summary: This study aimed to investigate clinical correlates of persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) in older adults, compare seven classification models, and interpret the selected gradient boosting machine (GBM) classifier. This single-center observational study included 572 adults reported to be aged ≥ 60 years who received care between June 2021 and June 2023, comprising 385 participants classified as having persistent AF and 187 comparators. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) were used for candidate-variable assessment and feature reduction. Logistic regression and six machine-learning models-support vector machine, GBM, neural network, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), AdaBoost, and CatBoost-were compared using a reported 70:30 development/test split and tenfold cross-validation during model development. Model performance and interpretation were examined using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), decision-curve analysis (DCA), and SHapley additive explanations (SHAP). The sequence of feature selection and data partitioning could not be verified. Fourteen candidate variables were significantly associated with persistent AF in univariable analysis, of which 9 remained significant after multivariable adjustment. LASSO retained 5 features: glycated hemoglobin, C2HEST score, heart failure, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and CO2. GBM achieved a development-set AUC of 0.970 (95% CI 0.957-0.983). In the test set, GBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost achieved AUCs of 0.919 (95% CI 0.874-0.963), 0.920 (95% CI 0.876-0.963), and 0.919 (95% CI 0.876-0.962), respectively. DCA suggested favorable net benefit for GBM across selected threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis identified ALT as the feature with the greatest contribution to GBM predictions, followed by the C2HEST score. GBM achieved the highest development-set AUC, whereas test-set AUCs were similar across GBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost. The five-feature classifier warrants further investigation for distinguishing persistent AF status in older adults. Verification of the analytical workflow, external validation, and calibration assessment are required before clinical application.

title: Development and validation of an explainable artificial intelligence model to predict in-hospital adverse events for patients with acute myocardial infarction.
summary: In-hospital adverse events after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can occur abruptly and adversely affect short-term prognosis. We developed and externally validated explainable machine learning models to predict a composite of in-hospital atrial fibrillation (AF), ventricular fibrillation (VF), cardiac arrest (CA), or death using routinely available admission data. We retrospectively analyzed 7,496 patients from the MIMIC-IV database as the development cohort and 2,776 patients from Xuanwu Hospital as the external validation cohort. Predictors included demographics, medical history, and admission laboratory tests. Logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), multilayer perceptron, and TabNet models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using discrimination, classification, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Latent class analysis identified three outcome clusters with distinct event-probability profiles. XGBoost achieved the best performance for the composite outcome in the development cohort (AUROC, 0.798). Predictive performance was moderate to good for AF and in-hospital death, with AUROCs of up to 0.834 and 0.870 in the development cohort and 0.803 and 0.849 in the external validation cohort, respectively. Discrimination was lower for VF and CA. SHapley Additive exPlanations highlighted neutrophil and leukocyte counts, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, renal function, glucose, glycated hemoglobin A1c, and prior AF as important predictors. These explainable models may support early risk stratification and help guide monitoring intensity and timely intervention in patients with AMI.

title: Retraction: Hydrogen decreases susceptibility to AngII-induced atrial fibrillation and atrial fibrosis via the NOX4/ROS/NLRP3 and TGF-β1/Smad2/3 signaling pathways.

Machine learning framework to enhance and automate cardiovascular outpatient triage for patients with atrial fibrillation.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia, placing a substantial burden on the healthcare system. Patients with AF are cared for in a variety of settings, including primary care and cardiovascular (CV) clinics, while some require cardiac electrophysiology (EP) clinics that offer specialized drugs or procedures. Triage of AF referrals to these specific clinics will lead to timely and proper care and reduce inefficiency in the health system. The goal is to develop a machine learning framework to triage the likelihood of patient referrals to EP-directed treatments.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 6,755 patients who were referred to CV with a referral diagnosis of AF. Data encompassed patient demographics, relevant comorbidities, medications, prior procedures, medical notes analyzed using natural language processing (NLP), and Holter monitoring data. A two-stage framework, predicting the necessity for specialized EP care, was developed: the construction of the machine learning model, followed by post-refinement based on established clinical criteria.

RESULTS: The Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) model emerged as the most effective model in the first stage, achieving an area under the curve of 0.77, an accuracy of 72%, a true positive rate (TPR) of 67%, and a false positive rate of 23%. The post-refinement stage further improved TPR to as much as 83%. This framework resulted in increased identification of EP-direct patient care from the current reported 20% to 46%.

CONCLUSIONS: Our framework effectively identifies patients who are likely to require specialized EP care, thereby enhancing the automation of the AF referral triage process and potentially improving efficiency.

title: Association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry and restrictive spirometric pattern with incident atrial fibrillation: a cohort study.
summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation (AF). To our knowledge, no studies have examined the association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) or restrictive spirometric pattern (RSP) with incident AF. We included participants without prevalent AF who had incident AF ascertainment and available spirometry and excluded those with airflow limitation. PRISm and RSP were evaluated as binary exposures and as four mutually exclusive spirometric patterns. Missing covariates were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations, and logistic regression estimates were pooled using Rubin's rules. Sensitivity analyses used an individual lower limit of normal (LLN) for the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio, complete-case analysis, and an alternative smoking model including pack-years and current smoking. A total of 2219 participants were included, with a mean age of 62.4 years, of whom 43.6% were male. During follow-up, 247 incident AF events (11.1%) were recorded. In fully adjusted models, PRISm was associated with incident AF (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.12, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.35-3.31, P = 0.001), and RSP was also associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.38, 95% CI 1.58-3.60, P < 0.001). When participants were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups, PRISm+RSP remained associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.62, 95% CI 1.63-4.22, P < 0.001), whereas PRISm alone (aOR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.21-2.81, P = 0.690) and RSP alone (aOR = 1.88, 95% CI 0.93-3.80, P = 0.077) were not statistically significant. Results were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Among adults without airflow limitation, binary PRISm and RSP were associated with higher odds of incident AF. In mutually exclusive analyses, the clearest association was observed in participants with concurrent reductions in FEV1 and FVC.

title: Electrical Storm Triggered by Conus Branch Occlusion During Elective Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Very Severe Aortic Stenosis: Rescue With Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty Under Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
summary: We report a case of very severe aortic stenosis (AS) in which side-branch occlusion during elective percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) precipitated life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and hemodynamic collapse. The patient was a 72-year-old man with very severe AS who was scheduled to undergo a valve intervention. Preprocedural coronary angiography revealed a significant, newly developed stenosis in the right coronary artery, and an elective PCI was performed prior to valve treatment. Following intravascular lithotripsy and drug-eluting stent implantation, occlusion of the conus branch occurred, triggering recurrent ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Despite initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and intra-aortic balloon pump support, the patient's hemodynamic status did not improve. Because excessive afterload due to very severe AS was considered the principal pathophysiological mechanism, emergency balloon aortic valvuloplasty was performed. This resulted in rapid hemodynamic stabilization and complete resolution of ventricular arrhythmias. This case illustrates that even a minor side-branch occlusion during PCI can lead to catastrophic outcomes in patients with very severe AS. Furthermore, it highlights that mechanical circulatory support alone may be insufficient, and that prompt relief of valvular obstruction is essential. Careful consideration of the indications and sequence of coronary intervention through discussions with a heart team is warranted for patients with very severe AS.

title: Vasospastic Angina and Cardiac Arrest.
summary: Vasospastic angina (VSA) is an important and potentially treatable cause of cardiac arrest (CA) and may account for approximately 2-10% of otherwise unexplained cases of out-of-hospital CA. VSA can sometimes be diagnosed by spontaneous coronary spasm during emergency coronary angiography or by transient ST-segment elevation during a spontaneous attack after resuscitation. However, because coronary spasm is transient and may not be evident during the initial evaluation, provocation testing after clinical stabilization may be required to establish the diagnosis in otherwise unexplained cases. Once VSA is diagnosed, vasodilator therapy, particularly calcium-channel blockers, is the mainstay of treatment. Nevertheless, survivors of VSA-related CA may remain at risk of recurrent lethal ventricular arrhythmias despite medical therapy. Evaluation for alternative or overlapping arrhythmogenic disorders, including cardiomyopathies and channelopathies, should therefore be considered even after a diagnosis of VSA, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation may be considered in selected patients according to the risk of recurrence and response to medical therapy. Further prospective studies, including randomized controlled trials, are needed to determine whether systematic provocation testing followed by targeted therapy reduces recurrent ventricular arrhythmias and CA and improves long-term outcomes.

title: Sudden Liberalization at F.A.A. and Concerns for Aviation Safety: Active Implantable-Defibrillators in the Cockpit? Really?
summary:
BACKGROUND: The health of pilots is essential for aviation safety and the well-being of passengers. Cardiovascular disease poses the greatest medical threat to flight safety and is the leading cause of lost certification for pilots.

METHODS: Public notification of a recent Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) decision granting licensure to pilots with cardiovascular disease and implanted defibrillators is notable.

RESULTS: A Delta Airlines first officer received a Class A pilot license despite experiencing a full cardiac arrest (with ventricular fibrillation) in the cockpit 6 h into a transatlantic flight at 40 000 feet, resulting in incapacitation and requiring (successful) cardiopulmonary resuscitation by the captain with an on-board emergency automatic external defibrillator. The pilot soon thereafter received an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden death. Electrophysiologic study demonstrated active LV arrhythmogenic foci leading to attempted myocardial ablation. After extensive litigation, the pilot was ultimately issued an unrestricted special issuance medical certificate, the first such FAA decision for a civilian pilot with an active implanted defibrillator and representing a major reversal of long-standing aeromedical policy and standards.

CONCLUSIONS: This novel liberalized practice of the FAA and NTSB as regulatory agencies, certifying at-risk pilots with active defibrillators that could deliver powerful appropriate therapy or inappropriate shocks in the cockpit, raises legitimate concerns regarding the impact of such decisions on aviation safety and the confidence of the flying public.

title: Shockingly Unreliable: A Case Report of Failure of Synchronized Cardioversion Device to Capture, Resulting in Ventricular Fibrillation and Cardiac Arrest.
summary:
Synchronized cardioversion is a standard treatment for unstable ventricular tachycardia. While modern defibrillators are designed with safety mechanisms, synchronization failure can result in catastrophic complications. We present the case of a 65-year-old woman with unstable wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse who underwent emergent synchronized cardioversion. Despite activation of the "sync" mode, the device failed to capture appropriately and delivered a shock on the T-wave, precipitating ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. After 26 minutes of resuscitation and multiple defibrillations, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved. The patient ultimately recovered and was discharged home in stable condition. This case underscores the rare but serious risk of synchronization failure, particularly in obese patients where pad placement and capture may be impaired,1 and emphasizes the importance of visually confirming synchronization prior to shock delivery.

TOPICS: Cardioversion, ventricular fibrillation, defibrillator malfunction, ACLS, emergency medicine.

title: Light-chain amyloidosis causing left ventricular outflow tract obstruction managed with a dual-chamber pacemaker: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Amyloid light-chain (AL) cardiac amyloidosis can rarely mimic hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve and resultant left ventricular (LV) outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO). Dual-chamber pacing with a right ventricular (RV) apical lead may be another option for LVOT gradient reduction and symptomatic relief for these patients.

CASE SUMMARY: A 67-year-old man presented with subacute bilateral lower extremity oedema and syncope. Examination revealed a systolic murmur increasing with Valsalva, bibasilar crackles, and pitting oedema. Electrocardiogram showed low QRS voltage disproportionate to the degree of LV wall thickening. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated severe concentric LV hypertrophy with SAM of the mitral valve and LVOTO (65 mmHg at rest, 100 mmHg with Valsalva). Laboratory tests and renal biopsy confirmed lambda AL amyloidosis, and endomyocardial biopsy confirmed cardiac amyloid infiltration. Medical therapy included cautious beta-blockade and midodrine, but the patient experienced refractory syncope. Septal reduction therapy was not anatomically feasible. Dual-chamber pacemaker implantation with RV apical pacing resulted in an improvement in the LVOT gradient and orthostatic symptoms. At more than 1 year after initiation of dual-chamber pacing and therapy directed at his underlying plasma cell dyscrasia, the patient had no further hospitalizations and endorsed sustained symptomatic improvement.

DISCUSSION: Management of LVOTO in patients with AL cardiac amyloidosis is challenging due to competing restrictive physiology and the absence of guideline-recommended practices. Dual-chamber pacing may reduce LVOT gradients and improve symptoms in cases refractory to medical management.

title: Upgrading right ventricular pacing to left bundle branch area pacing in pacemaker-induced cardiomyopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Chronic right ventricular pacing (RVP) causes pacemaker-induced cardiomyopathy (PICM) in 10-20% of patients. Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) restores His-Purkinje activation and offers an alternative upgrade strategy; however, no formal pooled analysis comparing LBBAP versus biventricular pacing (BiVP) exists.

METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Scopus from inception to March 2026, and pooled effect sizes using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) methods. Nine studies contributed to the single-arm meta-analysis; one further study (Huang et al.) provided comparative LBBAP-versus-BiVP data only. Full database-specific search strategies are provided in Supplemental Text S1.

RESULTS: Nine observational studies (N = 242) were eligible. LBBAP succeeded in 96.4% of the procedures (95% CI 92.2-99.3%). Pooled left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) improved by 11.72% points (95% CI + 9.85 to + 13.59), paced QRS narrowed by 51.83 ms, left ventricular end diastolic diameter (LVEDD) decreased by 4.10 mm (k = 5), and NYHA improved by 0.98 points (all p < 0.001). Three non-fatal device-related complications were recorded across 242 patients (pooled rate 1.8%). In two observational head-to-head studies (N = 170) - one of which (Huang et al.) contributed comparative data only and is not among the nine single-arm studies - LBBAP was associated with a 4.59%-point greater LVEF improvement than BiVP (95% CI + 2.23 to + 6.95); with only two nonrandomized studies, this comparison is hypothesis-generating. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the single-arm estimates.

CONCLUSION: LBBAP upgrade was associated with improvement in LVEF and symptoms in patients with PICM. Limited observational data suggest greater LVEF improvement with LBBAP than BiVP, but this finding remains hypothesis-generating. Adequately powered randomized trials with hard clinical endpoints are needed.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261381943) after the search but before data extraction: Upgrading right ventricular pacing to left bundle branch area pacing in pacemaker-induced cardiomyopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

title: The efficacy of add on cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) to symptomatic patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on sacubitril/valsartan treatment as regards left ventricle reverse remodeling and functional improvement.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Heart failure (HF) represents a substantial worldwide healthcare burden, with nearly 26 million people affected. CRT is widely recommended for HFrEF patients with QRS duration > 150 msec, but its role in those with QRS duration of 130-149 msec remains debated. The objective was to evaluate whether adding CRT improves LV reverse remodeling and functional status in symptomatic HFrEF patients receiving maximally tolerated sacubitril/valsartan with QRS duration of 130-149 msec.

METHODS: This study included 100 patients with HFrEF (≤ 35%) treated with maximally tolerated sacubitril/valsartan and having LBBB morphology with QRS duration of 130-149 msec. Patients were classified into two groups: those receiving CRT and those maintained on medical therapy without CRT. Clinical status, QRS duration, and echocardiographic findings were reassessed after 6 months and compared between groups.

RESULTS: At 6 months, NYHA class improvement occurred more frequently with CRT than without CRT (37 vs. 20 patients, P = 0.004). The decline in end-systolic volume was greater in the CRT group (mean change, 11.42 ± 7.30 vs. 3.54 ± 6.41, P < 0.001). Ejection fraction also showed greater improvement with CRT (mean change, 4.24 ± 3.17 vs. 1.30 ± 2.35, P < 0.001). Hospitalization occurred less frequently in the CRT group (46% vs. 70%, P = 0.03). No deaths were observed in either group throughout follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: In symptomatic HFrEF patients receiving maximally tolerated sacubitril/valsartan with QRS duration of 130-149 msec, adjunctive CRT was associated with greater LV reverse remodeling, improved functional status, and fewer hospitalizations.
